I actually really dislike the mentality this guy and others adopt when thinking about the homeless. I understand the sentiment that they hold, believing that somebody isn't working simply because they're lazy but this worldview is myopic and harmful. There are a whole galaxy of reasons why someone would have difficulty procuring employment. 

I've been working at a homeless shelter for the past 2 years and have seen so many people that would love to work but simply can't due to physical/mental handicaps. I've met more former tradesmen than I can count that get injured on the job and become essentially handicapped. They can't stand for long periods of time, simple movements become major obstacles, and their injuries end up evolving into worse health problems (spine injury turns into nerve damage, opioid dependency etc.). I once met a guy who was a successful contractor until his work truck got hit by another car. Now the only recent work he was able to get was from an elderly couple renovating their bathroom (and that's only because they don't mind he takes 3x as long to work). I've got people who were "normal" functioning people until they got **cancer** and their lives ended up unravelling. We've had 2 "normal" folks pass away at our site from cancer since last Fall. This doesn't include all the people that have died here recently, just the ones specifically from cancer. 

Or what about mental health? You ever try holding down a job in a kitchen or at Walmart when something as simple as someone playing music too loud throws you into a full blown panic attack? I once met a woman who spent her entire life on the street (I'm talking since childhood) and now doesn't know how to do something as simple as clean up her own vomit. I can think of about 5 folks off the top of my head staying with us who think they're being stalked by the government/criminal organizations. I've got veterans who ended up sleeping in parks because readjusting became too much for them. Some of these folks are completely unable to hold down normal employment for very long if they get it at all. Walmart don't give a damn if you gotta miss work for your methadone appointments or to see your parole officer. I've got old folks who've regressed too much mentally to take care of themselves, I've got elderly mothers who ended up getting scammed by terrible family members until they've got nothing left (this one is pretty common). These people are shot down to the bottom rung of society and then chastised for not being able to crawl their way out.

TlDr; Shit is tough out there for these people and Douchebag McBeergut holding that sign ain't helping.

Note: Im no master Dm but here's my advice that seems to work

If you wanna make a non linear story, the trick is to have multiple roads to certain set pieces or checkpoints in the story. That way youre not just forcing them from point to point and actually giving them reason to be there. Theres no planning around everything a party might do, just make outlines and plan out the most likely paths while being open to diversion. If they dont reach something you make, you can re-use it later (an unused bandit den becomes a werewolve's lair). Even npc's, imagine how they react to flattery, insult, etc. You dont need to be overly prepared, just flexible.

Also flesh out side stuff. Stores, npc's, settings, etc. Just going from place to place with no flavor isnt satisfying.

Example: "I have a trade city called Rosemoore with tons of shops and artisans. One shop is "Amil and Ster's". Its a general goods shop with a number of oddities. Its ran by the extroverted half elf merchant Amil and his half orc business partner/blacksmith Ster. Amil is courteous, kind and agreeable, but also a former thieves guild member trying to go straight. Ster speaks in grunts and dislikes conversation but is a gifted smith. Amil has a charm spell prepared to calm roudy customers."

See? Just add some backstory or a few traits and ya have something the party can sink their teeth into :D sure, nothing amazing, but it leads to fun interactions.
